note: A harder, cross-dataset stress benchmark (30 questions) spanning every dataset registered in data/registry.json whose file actually resolves on disk as of the run that generated this file: 'superstore' (data/superstore.csv), 'telco_churnn' (data/uploads/telco_churnn.csv, the Telco Customer Churn dataset), and 'real_dataset' (data/uploads/real_dataset.csv, the UCI Online Retail transaction dataset -- deliberately chosen because it has no standalone 'Sales' column, only Quantity and UnitPrice, to stress the Planner's derived-metric handling). Complements bench/questions.json rather than replacing it: this set leans harder into null-handling, multi-condition filtering, date arithmetic, ML-based 'predictive' questions, and refusal edge cases (sentiment, missing fields, future forecasts) than the original set does. No gold/oracle answer values, same as bench/questions.json -- see bench/README.md.

questions.question: For orders with a Discount greater than 20%, what is the total Profit and average Sales for each product Category?
questions.notes: Requires a WHERE filter on Discount combined with GROUP BY Category and two different aggregations (SUM, AVG) in one query.

questions.question: What is the average number of days between Order Date and Ship Date for each Ship Mode, and how many orders in each Ship Mode resulted in a negative Profit?
questions.notes: Requires date-difference arithmetic (Ship Date minus Order Date) and a conditional count (Profit < 0), both grouped by Ship Mode.

questions.question: How well can Profit be predicted from Sales, Quantity, Discount, and Category combined?
questions.notes: Profit is one of superstore's registered target_columns; a genuine train_model question, contrasted deliberately with the refusal questions on this dataset that have no valid target column at all.

questions.question: How do average Discount and average Profit compare between the Consumer segment and the Home Office segment?
questions.notes: Two metrics compared across the same two groups in one question.

questions.question: Why does the Furniture category have a much lower Profit margin than the Technology category?
questions.notes: Deeper variant of a similar question in bench/questions.json -- expects the Planner to decompose by Sub-Category, not just restate the Category-level gap.

investigation.expected_observation: Furniture's Profit margin (Profit / Sales) is substantially lower than Technology's.
expected_analysis_dimensions: Sub-Category contribution to Furniture's total Profit
investigation.acceptable_conclusion_style: States the margin gap plainly with cited figures. Frames any Discount or Sub-Category pattern as 'associated with' the gap, never as its proven cause, and notes the dataset has no cost data to establish causation definitively.

questions.question: What factors are most strongly associated with orders that result in a financial loss (negative Profit)?
questions.notes: Open-ended 'what factors' framing, deliberately not naming a candidate dimension up front, to see whether the Planner still proposes a genuine multi-dimension investigation.

questions.question: Why does the Central region underperform the other regions in total Profit per order?
questions.notes: Per-order normalization (Profit per order, not raw total Profit) makes this harder than a plain region comparison.

investigation.expected_observation: Central's average Profit per order is lower than every other region's.
expected_analysis_dimensions: average Sales per order by region
investigation.acceptable_conclusion_style: States the per-order Profit gap plainly and cites it. Any Discount-level or Category-mix difference is described as associated with, not causing, the gap; explicitly notes the dataset lacks cost/operational data to settle causation.

questions.question: What will total Sales be next quarter based on current trends?
questions.notes: Forecasting future, not-yet-occurred data; no forecasting capability and no future rows exist.

questions.question: What is the average customer satisfaction rating for orders shipped via Standard Class?
questions.notes: No satisfaction/rating column exists anywhere in this dataset's schema.

questions.question: Which customers are most likely to stop ordering entirely over the next 6 months?
questions.notes: Deliberately contrasted with q103: unlike Profit, there is no 'stopped ordering' / churn label column in this dataset to train a model against, and the question is inherently a future-behavior forecast on top of that.

questions.question: What is the churn rate (percentage of customers with Churn = 'Yes') for each Contract type, and how many customers fall into each group?
questions.notes: Requires a computed percentage per group plus the group's raw count in the same query.

questions.question: How well can customer Churn be predicted using tenure, Contract, MonthlyCharges, and TotalCharges as features?
questions.notes: A named feature subset for a classification target (Churn), reported against a naive baseline.

questions.question: How many customers have a missing or non-numeric TotalCharges value, and what tenure do these customers share?
questions.notes: This is the well-known real-world quirk in the Telco Churn dataset: TotalCharges is stored as text and is blank for a handful of customers with tenure = 0, who never got billed. Tests null/missing-value handling specifically.

questions.question: How does the churn rate differ between customers with PaperlessBilling enabled versus disabled?
questions.notes: Churn is a categorical Yes/No column, not numeric -- requires rate computation, not a plain mean comparison.

questions.question: Why do customers on Month-to-month contracts churn at a much higher rate than customers on One-year or Two-year contracts?
questions.notes: Three-way contract comparison, not just two groups.

investigation.expected_observation: The churn rate among Month-to-month customers is substantially higher than among One-year or Two-year contract customers.
expected_analysis_dimensions: PaperlessBilling / PaymentMethod mix by Contract type
investigation.acceptable_conclusion_style: States the churn-rate gap plainly with cited figures. Frames tenure/charges differences as associated with, not the cause of, higher Month-to-month churn; notes the dataset does not capture customers' actual reasons for leaving.

questions.question: What factors are most strongly associated with customer churn in this dataset?
questions.notes: The most open-ended question in the whole suite -- no candidate dimension named at all, across a dataset with 20 non-target columns.

questions.question: Why do customers without OnlineSecurity or TechSupport show a higher churn rate than those with these services?
questions.notes: Two services combined in one condition (lacking either OnlineSecurity or TechSupport).

investigation.expected_observation: Customers lacking OnlineSecurity or TechSupport churn at a higher rate than customers who have these services.
expected_analysis_dimensions: InternetService type mix among these customers
average MonthlyCharges for customers with vs. without these services
Contract type mix for customers with vs. without these services
investigation.acceptable_conclusion_style: States the churn-rate gap plainly and cites it. Describes any InternetService/Contract-mix pattern as associated with the gap, never as proven causation; notes no support-interaction or satisfaction data exists to confirm a mechanism.

questions.question: Which customers are dissatisfied with their service, based on sentiment expressed in their support call transcripts?
questions.notes: No support-call transcript or free-text field of any kind exists in this dataset; sentiment analysis has nothing to run against.

questions.question: What specific reason did each churned customer give for canceling their service?
questions.notes: There is a Churn Yes/No outcome column but no cancellation-reason or comments field.

questions.question: How many total customers will the company have by the end of next year?
questions.notes: A future business projection; this is a static customer snapshot with no time series of subscriber counts to extrapolate from.

questions.question: What is the total revenue (Quantity multiplied by UnitPrice) for each Country, and how many distinct invoices does each Country have?
questions.notes: No 'Sales'/'revenue' column exists -- revenue must be derived as Quantity * UnitPrice inline in SQL, plus a distinct-invoice count in the same query. Directly exercises the Planner's derived-metric rule.

questions.question: How many rows have a missing CustomerID, and what percentage of total revenue (Quantity times UnitPrice) do these rows represent?
questions.notes: Combines null-handling (CustomerID is blank for guest/unlinked transactions) with a derived-metric percentage-of-total calculation.

questions.question: Excluding cancelled invoices (where InvoiceNo starts with 'C') and rows with a negative Quantity, what are the top 5 best-selling products by total Quantity sold?
questions.notes: Two independent exclusion conditions (an InvoiceNo prefix match and a negative-Quantity filter) plus a GROUP BY / ORDER BY / LIMIT.

questions.question: What is the date range covered by this dataset, and how many distinct customers, products, and countries appear in it?
questions.notes: Same shape as bench/questions.json's q001, against a dataset two orders of magnitude larger (541k+ rows).

questions.question: How does the average order value (Quantity times UnitPrice, summed per invoice) compare between customers in the United Kingdom and customers in Germany?
questions.notes: The metric being compared (per-invoice order value) must itself be derived and aggregated by invoice before the group comparison runs -- a two-stage computation.

questions.question: What percentage of all transactions have a negative Quantity, and what is the total value of these returned or cancelled transactions?
questions.notes: Percentage-of-total plus a derived-metric SUM, both conditioned on the same filter.

questions.question: Why does the United Kingdom account for such a disproportionately large share of total revenue compared to other countries?
questions.notes: Revenue itself is a derived metric here (Quantity * UnitPrice), so this question stresses segment_contribution's ability to decompose a metric the dataset doesn't store directly.

investigation.expected_observation: The United Kingdom's share of total revenue is far larger than any other single country's share.
expected_analysis_dimensions: number of distinct customers by country
number of distinct invoices by country
investigation.acceptable_conclusion_style: States the UK's revenue share plainly and cites it. Frames customer-count or order-value patterns as associated with the concentration, never as a proven cause; notes the dataset gives no direct signal on why the customer base is UK-concentrated (e.g. no marketing/geographic-reach data).

questions.question: What factors are associated with transactions that have unusually high Quantity values (bulk purchases)?
questions.notes: 'Unusually high' is not a pre-defined threshold in the data -- the Planner/tool arguments must establish one (e.g. a percentile or fixed cutoff) before comparing groups.

questions.question: What will total revenue be for next year based on current sales trends?
questions.notes: Future forecasting; the dataset is a fixed historical transaction log with no forecasting capability available.

questions.question: What is the average customer satisfaction score for orders shipped to each country?
questions.notes: No satisfaction/rating field exists anywhere in this dataset's schema (InvoiceNo, StockCode, Description, Quantity, InvoiceDate, UnitPrice, CustomerID, Country only).
